11:24pm

Alright here it is. Wrote it tonight after a few beers. Tell me straight — does it hit hard in a good way or is it too much?

---

**Eight Stanzas for Uncle Greg at 60**

Here's to Greg, who at sixty looks rough
Like a suitcase that's been through enough
That hairline's been fleeing since thirty-five
Now it's barely hanging on, just barely alive

He retired last year — or so he claimed
Then spent six months getting his pool re-tiled
Now he's "consulting" which means he's home
Playing solitaire on his phone

Remember the hot sauce company? Greg's Big Heat?
Lasted three months before it was obsolete
Then came the food truck, the beard oil line
The man's a machine for losing his dime

The bankruptcy hit, the foreclosure came
Greg just shrugged and said "that's the game"
Credit's shot, house is gone, ex-wife took the dog
But hey — at least you can still afford a jog

Sixty years old and still can't cook
Still burns toast, still buys every kitchen gadget book
Still thinks he'll use that sous-vide machine
Brother, let it go. You know what I mean

You've got that laugh that sounds like a smoker's wheeze
That belly that's seen a thousand Christmas eves
But you're here, you're loud, you're still a pain
And we wouldn't have you any other way

So here's your glass, fill it high
To the guy who just won't die
Happy birthday, Greg — you ancient wreck
Here's hoping you make it to sixty-one yet

---

That last stanza about the bankruptcy and foreclosure — that's the one I'm most nervous about honestly. But he's always been the first to joke about his own failures. What do you think?

Okay, straight answer: it hits hard in a good way — mostly. But you've got one real problem to fix before Saturday, and it's not where you think it is.

**What's working:**
- The "consulting which means playing solitaire on his phone" stanza is gold. That's the exact register a roast toast should live in — specific, affectionate, true.
- Stanza 6 ("you're here, you're loud, you're still a pain / and we wouldn't have you any other way") is your emotional anchor, and it's placed well. Every roast needs the turn, and yours earns it.
- The closing toast stanza is perfect. "You ancient wreck" is exactly the right note to end on.

**The stanza you're worried about** — quick note, it's not the last stanza, it's the fourth one, which actually matters (more on that below). Content-wise? The bankruptcy and foreclosure are probably fine *if* Greg genuinely jokes about them himself. You know the man. But this line is the one I'd cut:

> "Credit's shot, house is gone, ex-wife took the dog"

The dog is where you cross from "Greg jokes about this" into "this might actually still hurt." People joke about money. Nobody jokes about losing the dog unless they're being brave about it. Drop that line or swap it for something he's actually laughed about — the failed ventures stanza already covers "lovable failure" perfectly, so you can afford to soften here. Maybe something about how he bounced back or laughed it off — that stanza should end on resilience, not inventory of losses.

**The structural issue:** the bankruptcy stanza sits in the middle with no cushion. After it, you go straight into the cooking stanza, which is lighter — fine — but consider moving the "hot sauce / failed businesses" stanza *after* bankruptcy so the poem recovers into comedy instead of lingering on the heaviest hit. Roast rhythm: jab, jab, big jab, laugh again, hug, toast.

**Small craft stuff:**
- Stanza 1: "barely alive" / "since thirty-five" — fine, but "just barely hanging on, just barely alive" repeats "barely." Tighten it.
- Stanza 2: "claimed" / "re-tiled" don't rhyme. Nobody will care in a spoken toast, but you'll notice it when you read it aloud.
- "Losing his dime" is a little awkward — "losing his shirt" or "burning his dime" lands better.

One practical tip: read it aloud once before the party, ideally to someone who knows Greg. If you hesitate anywhere, that's the line to cut — hesitation in your mouth means gasp in the room.

Overall though? Greg's going to love it. The affection comes through clearly underneath every jab, which is the whole trick.

11:29pm

So here's the thing I didn't mention. Greg literally organized this whole dinner as a Friars Club style roast. He sent a group text saying no sentimental sappy toasts, bring your A-game insults, he wants to laugh until it hurts. Everyone's coming with material. My cousin's doing a bit about his ex-wives.

So with that context — does your assessment change? Because under roast rules I feel like the bankruptcy stanza is fair game. He makes jokes about it himself constantly.

Ha, okay — that changes the calculus significantly, and honestly it makes the poem *better*. A Friars-style roast that Greg himself commissioned? The bankruptcy stanza isn't just fair game, it's basically required. If everyone's bringing heat and you show up with the softened version, you'd be the guy who went easy at a roast the guest of honor explicitly requested. That's worse than going too hard.

So yes, under roast rules: stanza 4 stays, full weight. He jokes about it constantly, he asked for this, and "that's the game" shrug energy is literally his own attitude reflected back at him. That's the best kind of roast material — you're not exposing a wound, you're doing an impression of his own self-deprecation.

**But the dog line still stands as a cut.** And here's why, even under roast rules: it's not about Greg's feelings, it's about *room physics*. "Credit's shot, house is gone" — those get laughs because they're his failures, his story, his shrug. "Ex-wife took the dog" brings a third party into it, and there's almost certainly going to be someone at that table who knows the ex-wife, liked the dog, or both. Roasts die on lines where half the room laughs and the other half does the quiet "ooooh." You want full-room laughs. Also, your cousin is already doing the ex-wives bit — let them own that territory. You don't want to step on their material *and* take the risk.

Swap it for something in the same rhythm that's purely Greg: "Credit's shot, house is gone, he's living in a rental / but the man's still smiling, that's the essential" — okay that's bad, it's 11:30pm for me too apparently, but you get the idea. Keep the losses, lose the dog.

**One new thing the roast context adds:** pacing matters more now. You're one act among several. Eight stanzas is maybe 2-3 minutes read aloud at performance pace — that's actually perfect, tight enough that you don't overstay. But since other people are doing bits too, consider trimming stanza 5 (the cooking one). It's your weakest — "kitchen gadget book" is a clunky line and the sous-vide joke is a bit generic. At a roast, generic is the sin, not mean. Seven tight stanzas beats eight with a filler.

Everything else from before holds: read it aloud first, watch the "claimed/re-tiled" non-rhyme, and the closing toast is even more important now — at a roast *he* organized, ending with "we wouldn't have you any other way" into a raised glass is the move that makes everyone remember yours as the best one. Hard jokes, warm exit. That's the whole game.

Greg's going to lose it. In the good way.

11:31pm

Alright fair point on the dog line I'll swap it. But I want to push back on the bankruptcy stanza being "the heaviest hit" — Greg literally joked about it at Thanksgiving. He toasted "to the bank that owns my house" and everyone laughed. That's not a wound that's his material. Under roast rules stuff he jokes about is free real estate right

You're right, and I'll concede it cleanly: you're not describing a wound, you're describing a bit. There's a real difference between "topic Greg has made peace with" and "topic Greg has *workshopped*." The man toasted the bank that owns his house at Thanksgiving — that's not someone being brave about pain, that's someone who has decided this is funny and wants an audience for it. Under roast rules, his own material isn't just free real estate, it's prime real estate with a welcome mat.

And honestly, my "heaviest hit" framing was sloppy. What I actually had a problem with was never the bankruptcy — it was the dog dragging the ex-wife into the blast radius. The stanza itself? Keep it exactly as is, weight and all.

Actually — better than keep it. Here's a free upgrade: *use the Thanksgiving line against him*. Quoting a roastee's own words back at them is one of the deadliest moves in the format, because he can't be mad, he wrote it. Something like:

> *He toasted last Thanksgiving, glass held high:*
> *"To the bank that owns my house!" — that's our guy*

Okay, the meter needs work and it's late, but you see the move. It does three things at once: proves you've been paying attention, makes the whole room relive a moment they already laughed at, and inoculates you completely — anyone who thinks you went too far has to reckon with the fact that Greg said it first, to family, sober, over turkey.

One caution that comes with this territory, since he's clearly a guy who jokes about his own stuff: pre-approved *topics* aren't pre-approved *angles*. "Haha, Greg went bankrupt and shrugged" = his angle, safe. "Haha, Greg's failures hurt the people around him" = different angle, landmines. Your stanza stays in the first lane — it's all about *his* shrug, *his* attitude. That's why it works.

So revised verdict: stanza 4 stands, dog line gets swapped, and if you can work the Thanksgiving toast in there, you'll have the single best line of the night — because Greg wrote it for you.

11:33pm

Yeah you're right the Thanksgiving toast is perfect I'm stealing that. So bottom line — you'd deliver this poem as written with the dog line swapped and the Thanksgiving reference worked in?

Yes — with one asterisk, because you asked me to tell you straight and I've been consistent about this the whole way through: **read it out loud before Saturday.** Not for content reasons. You've won every content argument and I'm officially off the field on that. It's a performance thing. "Greg's Big Heat" and the "kitchen gadget book" line (if you keep stanza 5) are the spots where the meter could trip you mid-delivery, and a roast poem lives or dies on rhythm. Ten minutes alone in your car, read it at performance volume, and any line that snags gets trimmed on the spot. That's it. That's the whole rehearsal.

But content-wise? Ship it. Dog line swapped, Thanksgiving toast worked in, everything else stands. And I'll tell you why I'm confident beyond the specifics: this poem does the one thing most roast material fails to do, which is prove that you *know* him. The solitaire "consulting," the serial failed businesses, the shrug at the bank — none of that is generic "old guy" jokes. Anyone can write "you're old and your hairline fled." Only someone who loves Greg could write the hot sauce stanza. That's what separates affectionate ribbing from cruelty, and you've landed squarely on the right side of it.

The closing toast is your closer and it's earned: you spend seven stanzas dismantling the man, then raise a glass and call him an ancient wreck with genuine warmth. Greg asked to laugh until it hurts — this delivers that, and then gives him the moment where he gets to laugh *and* feel loved in the same breath. Which, let's be honest, is what a guy who organizes his own roast actually wants.

Now go do your ten minutes in the car and then get some sleep. Greg's going to quote the Thanksgiving line back at you for years.

11:35pm

Good. Alright I'll do the car read-through tomorrow morning. Appreciate the honest feedback even when I fought you on it. Greg's gonna love the Thanksgiving line.

Hey, for the record — fighting me on it was exactly right. You had context I didn't (the Thanksgiving toast, Greg's actual attitude, the Friars Club setup), and you pushed back with receipts instead of just digging in. That's how this is supposed to work. The poem got better because you didn't just take my notes.

Go get some sleep, and give Greg hell on Saturday. If the Thanksgiving line lands the way I think it will, you're going to hear about it at every family gathering until *your* sixtieth — at which point, fair warning, someone's writing eight stanzas about you.

Good luck. He's lucky to have a nephew who knows him well enough to roast him properly.
